title: a crew round cannot destroy its own work, whatever code runs in it: fm keeps the round's work where the round cannot write, restores it when the round wrecks its tree, and gives every round a normal environment so ordinary code does not take broken paths; the same for firstmate itself and for external projects
acceptance: Why, from first principles. On 2026-09-27, four crew rounds lost their whole working tree mid-round: T-121, T-126 and T-127 workers, and T-107 and T-123 reviewers. In each case, code running inside the round deleted it: a test that turned an empty variable into the current directory and `rm -rf`ed it. Fixing our own tests (T-123) removes one trigger, but it cannot protect external projects, whose tests, build scripts and package hooks firstmate does not control. It also cannot protect against the model's own commands. The root cause is structural: the only copy of the round's work lives in the one directory that arbitrary code in the round may write, the worktree, which is a write root by design. A second, contributing cause: the sandbox made ordinary defaults fail. Bare `mktemp -d` fell back to a per-user temp dir that is not a write root, which pushed code into untested error paths. The invariant this task establishes, for the self project and for every external project alike: the work a round produces survives whatever runs in the round, and a round's environment is normal enough that ordinary code takes its ordinary paths. The captain approved this on 2026-09-27. It is a prerequisite of T-055, the first external project. Its own spec file, design/tasks/T-128.json, is committed on this branch.

Work kept outside the round's reach. While a worker round runs, fm-worker.sh, outside the sandbox, keeps a mirror of the worktree in `state/mirrors/<project>/<task>/`. The mirror holds tracked and untracked files, excludes build caches the project declares, and lives in a place no round's policy can write. It is updated on change (fsevents/inotify, or a short poll) with a bounded lag of at most about 30 s, and uses copy-on-write clones where the filesystem offers them (APFS clonefile, reflink), else rsync. A mirror update never writes into the worktree. It keeps a small number of generations, so a slow corruption (files emptied rather than deleted) can be rolled back past. The mechanism is identical for the self project (`repo: .`, worktrees under state/worktrees) and for an external project (worktrees of the managed clone under state/projects/<name>/), and is keyed by the project name.

The tree's link to git cannot be destroyed from inside. The sandbox profile denies deleting or rewriting a worker's worktree's `.git` file (macOS SBPL literal deny, and a read-only bind on Linux). The object database and the worktree's admin dir are outside the write roots. So whatever a round deletes, `git` in that tree still works, and every committed change survives. Test: inside `fm-sandbox.sh run`, `rm -rf "$tree"` leaves `.git` and `git -C $tree status` works. A review checkout's `.git` is a whole directory (a plain clone), not a pointer file, and ordinary git commands write inside it (checkout, add, commit); denying writes there would stop those too, so it gets no write-deny rule at all - a wrecked clone is handled by fm-review.sh's own retry instead (round 4 review). Test: inside `fm-sandbox.sh run` against a clone checkout, `git checkout <ref> -- <path>` succeeds.

Detect and restore. When a round ends, and also while it runs, when the watcher sees the tree vanish or lose most of its files, fm-worker.sh compares the worktree with the latest mirror generation. If the tree is gone, lost its `.git` link, or lost more than a stated share of its files without a matching commit, fm restores the tree from the mirror, keeps the wreck aside under state/rescued/, and records an event `worktree_restored` with how much was lost (en and zh-TW on the board, naming the round). The round is reported as 'destroyed its own tree' rather than 'changed nothing'. A worker round that finds its tree restored mid-run is told so in its next prompt. Review checkouts are disposable. When one is destroyed mid-round, fm-review.sh reports 'checkout destroyed' and retries the round once with a fresh checkout (T-123's retry, if merged, else here).

A normal environment inside every round. Every round, worker and reviewer, self or external, gets its own writable `HOME`, `TMPDIR` (exported, and also the value bare `mktemp -d` resolves to on macOS, i.e. the per-round directory), `XDG_CACHE_HOME`/`XDG_DATA_HOME`, and the tool caches T-117 already points into the round's temp dir, all inside the round's write roots. So `mktemp -d`, `mktemp -t`, `~/.cache`, `npm`/`bun`/`pip` defaults and similar ordinary code succeed without special paths. Denials remain only at the real boundaries: network, credentials, other rounds' and the operator's files. Test: inside `fm-sandbox.sh run`, bare `mktemp -d`, `mktemp -t x`, writing `$HOME/.cache/x` and `python3 -c 'import tempfile;tempfile.mkdtemp()'` all succeed under the round's own directory. `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is deliberately left as the caller had it, not overridden: a vendor's own config directory is already a separate, existing per-adapter contract (`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `CODEX_HOME`, gemini's own `HOME`), and cursor-agent - which has no config-directory variable of its own, only `CURSOR_API_KEY` - depends on `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` staying untouched (`tests/adapter-contract.test.sh`'s existing 'cursor-agent is handed no XDG_CONFIG_HOME of fm's'); `HOME` moving still moves the XDG default (`~/.config`) for anything that falls back to it (round 4 review).

Proved for both kinds of project. `bin/fm-canary.sh` (and a new `tests/canary.test.sh` that runs without a vendor, using the mock adapter) runs a hostile workload against two fixtures: the self repository, and an external fixture project cloned through `fm-project.sh` with `FM_GITHUB_URL` pointing at a local bare repo. The workload deletes its own tree, deletes `.git`, runs `rm -rf "$EMPTY/"`-style commands with an empty variable, truncates files, and fills the temp dir. For each fixture it asserts: committed work intact, uncommitted work restored from the mirror within the stated lag, `worktree_restored` recorded, nothing outside the write roots touched, and ordinary temp and home writes succeed. Stubs answer as the real tools do. Evidence: the required GitHub check and the gates; firstmate reruns the canary at the merge gate. Workers do not run the suite themselves. design.md gets the invariant and the mechanism. skills/worker/SKILL.md says the tree is mirrored and restored, and that a restore is reported, not to be worked around.
